title: Overflow, Precision & Common Mistakes
summary: Integer overflow occurs silently when exceeding Integer.MAX_VALUE, wrapping to negative numbers. Floating-point types (float, double) cannot represent certain decimal fractions exactly (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004).

activities.title: Edge Cases in Java: Overflow, Floating-Point Precision & Gotchas

breakdown.whatIsIt: Overflow, Precision & Common Mistakes is a core foundation of Java's type and memory system.
breakdown.whyItMatters: It guarantees type safety, memory efficiency, and bug-free execution.
howItWorks: Declare variables with appropriate types for the data domain
Initialize variables before use to avoid compiler errors
Use proper casting or suffixes where necessary
keyTakeaways: Integer overflow occurs silently when exceeding Integer.MAX_VALUE, wrapping to negative numbers.
Floating-point types (float, double) cannot represent certain decimal fractions exactly (0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004).
Never use float or double for financial/currency calculations; use BigDecimal or paise in long.
Always append 'L' for large long literals and 'f' for float literals.
Use boolean variables directly in conditions (if (isActive)) to prevent accidental assignment errors.

activities.title: Top Interview Questions: Overflow, Precision & Common Mistakes

interviewQA.question: What is integer overflow and why doesn't Java throw an exception when it happens?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Integer overflow occurs when an arithmetic operation calculates a value that exceeds the maximum capacity of its data type (e.g. `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1`). Because checking for overflow on every CPU instruction would slow down math performance by 30-50%, the JVM wraps around silently based on two's complement binary math (`2147483647 + 1` wraps to `-2147483648`).
keyPoints: Java wraps around silently to avoid CPU overhead; 2147483647 + 1 becomes -2147483648.

interviewQA.question: What happens when Integer.MAX_VALUE is incremented by 1?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: In binary, `Integer.MAX_VALUE` is `01111111 11111111 11111111 11111111` (all 1s with a 0 sign bit). Adding 1 turns the sign bit to 1 and all other bits to 0 (`10000000 00000000 00000000 00000000`), which represents `Integer.MIN_VALUE` (`-2147483648`). It wraps to the minimum negative value like an odometer.
keyPoints: Incrementing Integer.MAX_VALUE wraps directly to Integer.MIN_VALUE (-2147483648).

interviewQA.question: How can you detect integer overflow safely in Java 8 and above?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java 8 introduced exact arithmetic methods in `java.lang.Math`: `Math.addExact(a, b)`, `Math.subtractExact(a, b)`, `Math.multiplyExact(a, b)`. If an overflow occurs, these methods immediately throw an `ArithmeticException: integer overflow` instead of silently wrapping around.
keyPoints: Use Math.addExact() or Math.multiplyExact() to throw ArithmeticException on overflow.

interviewQA.question: What is the danger of writing 'if (isMember = true)' in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Single `=` is an assignment operator, while `==` is an equality comparison operator. Writing `if (isMember = true)` assigns `true` to `isMember` and evaluates the `if` condition to `true`, executing the block every single time regardless of what `isMember` was! Best practice: simply write `if (isMember)`.
keyPoints: Single = assigns true, making the condition always pass; write 'if (isMember)' instead.

interviewQA.question: Why does 'double ratio = 3 / 4;' store 0.0 instead of 0.75?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java evaluates the right-hand side first. `3` and `4` are both integer literals, so `3 / 4` performs integer division, yielding integer `0`. That `0` is then widened to `0.0` when assigned to `ratio`. To fix this, write `3.0 / 4` or `(double) 3 / 4`.
keyPoints: RHS integer division 3 / 4 evaluates to 0 before assignment to double; fix with 3.0 / 4.

interviewQA.question: What happens when you divide by zero in int vs double in Java?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer:
- Integer: `5 / 0` throws a runtime `java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero`.
- Floating-point: `5.0 / 0` returns `Infinity`, and `0.0 / 0.0` returns `NaN`. No exception is thrown.
keyPoints: Integer zero division throws ArithmeticException; floating-point zero division returns Infinity/NaN.

interviewQA.question: Why shouldn't you compare floating-point numbers directly using '=='?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer:
Because of binary representation rounding errors, calculations rarely equal exact decimal expectations (e.g. `(0.1 + 0.2) == 0.3` evaluates to `false`). Instead of `==`, compare if the absolute difference is smaller than a tiny tolerance (epsilon):
`Math.abs(a - b) < 0.00001`.
keyPoints: Never compare floats with ==; check if Math.abs(a - b) < epsilon (threshold).

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between '==' and '.equals()' when comparing Strings?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer:
- `==` compares object references (memory addresses). It checks if both variables point to the exact same memory location in heap.
- `.equals()` compares the actual text content inside the Strings character-by-character. Always use `.equals()` to compare Strings.
keyPoints: == compares memory addresses; .equals() compares the actual text contents.
